330.title: The first mountain, from the top
330.hook: you've been climbing for 329 days: today, turn around and look down the trail
330.howItsDone: Many Hindus mark the end of a period of study or a vow with a pause to look back, often with a puja or a visit to a teacher to give thanks; people who finish reading the whole Gita sometimes celebrate its completion.

segments.voice: Last week, five houses heard in their own words, then two questions at your own door: a thread on the wrist, and what to do when someone isn't kind. Your line was your worth isn't up for a vote.
screen: `YOUR WORTH ISN'T UP FOR A VOTE.`

segments.voice: Near the top of a long climb, there's a moment. You've been staring at your feet for hours: the next rock, the next root, the next switchback. Your legs hurt. You haven't looked up in a long time. Then the trail flattens, there's nowhere higher to step, and you turn around. The whole path is lying there below you, the parking lot tiny, the first bend you thought was steep looking like nothing at all. You did that, one step a day. Today there's no new idea. Today, you turn around.
screen: `EYES ON YOUR FEET FOR MONTHS.` → `THE TRAIL FLATTENS.` → `TURN AROUND.`

segments.voice: Look down the trail. At the very bottom, camp one: twenty-one words. Namaste, om, dharma, shanti, karma, atman, Brahman, seva, bhakti, moksha, and the others. Some you may have said for years without knowing what they meant; some were new. Either way, they were Sanskrit. A little higher, camp two: the stories. Ganesha and his broken tusk. Hanuman's leap. The whole Ramayana as a serial, Rama and Sita and the long road home. Then the Mahabharata's cliffhangers, leaving two armies on a field. Higher still, camp three: the practices. Breath, mantra, a small shrine, a flame at sunset, food as offering, the temple, the festivals. The path stopped being something you listened to and became something you did. Then the steep part, camp four: the Bhagavad Gita, all eighteen chapters, about seven hundred verses, read in order. Arjuna dropping his bow. Krishna's answer. Chapter eleven's terrifying vision. And at the end, Krishna handing the choice back to Arjuna: do as you choose. You read the whole thing. The last stretch, camp five: the depths. The Upanishads, Isha, Kena, Katha, Mandukya. The three paths of action, devotion and knowledge. Advaita and Dvaita side by side, never ranked. The Yoga Sutras' first line: now, yoga. A track of your own choosing. And last week, a guest in five other houses. That's the first mountain, not the whole range. A traditional teacher might say you haven't finished anything; you've just learned to walk. But from up here, the steps add up.
screen: `CAMP ONE: TWENTY-ONE WORDS.` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `CAMP FOUR: THE WHOLE GITA.` · `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS.` · then, large: `LOOK HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the year come back, one breath at a time: a word from camp one; a story, a monkey, a bridge, a chariot; something you did, a flame, a mantra, a meal; one line from the Gita that stayed; one question from the depths, who am I? Then just rest at the top.
Shikhara, a mountain peak. Twenty-one words, the stories, the practices, the whole Gita and the depths, held for two minutes at once, the way a view holds a trail.
Your line: look how far. One step a day, and it got you all the way here. Day three hundred thirty.

331.title: Year one close
331.hook: from the top of the first mountain, you can see the next ones: the Upanishads, the Ramayana, the Yoga Sutras, your track
331.howItsDone: Hindu study is traditionally lifelong: people return to the Upanishads, the epics and the Gita again and again, often with a teacher, and many families hear the Ramayana or the Bhagavata Purana recited over days or weeks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shikhara, the whole year held in one sit: words, stories, practices, the Gita, the depths. Your line was look how far.

A minute after you turn around at the top, a second thing happens. You've looked at the trail. You've caught your breath. Then you turn back the other way, and you see it. Behind this peak, there's another. And behind that one, a whole line of them, blue and white, going on past where your eyes can follow. The first mountain was the one you could see from the parking lot. The ranges were hiding behind it the whole time. This is the last day of year one. Today, what's ahead.
screen: `THE SECOND MINUTE AT THE TOP.` → `ANOTHER PEAK, THEN ANOTHER.` → `THE LAST DAY OF YEAR ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with where you stand. Year one gave you the vocabulary, the stories, the practices, one complete scripture read straight through, in order, and a first look at the depths. That's a real thing. Now look ahead. The first range is the rest of the principal Upanishads. You met four of them this year. Year two opens the others, beginning tomorrow with the Chandogya and its teaching on om, which it calls the essence of essences. Later in that range come lines Hindus still quote, like the Chandogya's tat tvam asi: you are that. The second range is the Ramayana again, this time as a year-long serial, the full story, slowly, the way families once heard it over many evenings. The third is the Yoga Sutras complete: all one hundred ninety-five short threads of Patanjali, not just the opening. Then your lineage track in full, whichever you walked. And behind those, farther off: the Mahabharata as a serial, the Puranas, the saints and poets from the Alvars to Kabir to Vivekananda. Nobody climbs all of that in a week, and the texts themselves don't pretend you would. The Katha Upanishad, which you read this year, tells the seeker to arise, awake, and learn from those who know, and it says the path is as sharp as a razor's edge and hard to cross. It never says the path is short. It says to get up, wake up, and find someone who knows the way.
screen: `WHERE YOU STAND: THE FIRST MOUNTAIN.` · `THE REST OF THE UPANISHADS.` · `THE RAMAYANA, THE YOGA SUTRAS, YOUR TRACK.` · `ARISE, AWAKE: THE PATH IS LONG.` · then, large: `THE RANGES AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Last sit of year one: sit tall, like someone at the top of a hill, and feel what you carry now that you didn't carry a year ago, a word, a story, a habit, a question. Then turn, in your mind, toward the ranges; you don't have to know how you'll climb them, just see them there, patient as mountains are. If you pray, you can bring your own thanks for the year.
Himalaya, the abode of snow. The great range still ahead: the rest of the Upanishads, the Ramayana as a serial, the Yoga Sutras complete, your lineage track in full, and farther peaks behind them.
Your line: there's more. There's always more. That's day three hundred thirty-one, and year one.

332.title: The udgitha — om as the essence of essences (1.1)
332.hook: year two opens the Chandogya Upanishad, and its very first line says: meditate on om, the high chant
332.tomorrow: speech and breath argue about who is greatest
332.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant om at the start and end of prayer, study and puja; in traditional Vedic schools, students of the Sama Veda still learn the Chandogya's chants by ear from a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Himalaya, the abode of snow, and your line, there's more. There's always more. Year two starts now, with the first range.

Year two opens beside a fire. In the old Vedic sacrifice, priests sit around a fire on an altar, each with a job. One pours the offerings. One recites the verses. And one, the singer, waits for his moment, then lifts his voice into a long, rising chant: the udgitha, the high song. It was his whole craft. Now suppose someone in that circle asked a strange question. Not how do you sing it, but what is it, really? What is the song made of? The Chandogya Upanishad, where year two begins, opens with an answer.
screen: `A FIRE, A CIRCLE OF PRIESTS.` → `THE SINGER'S HIGH SONG.` → `WHAT IS IT MADE OF?`

segments.voice: The Chandogya belongs to the Sama Veda, the Veda of chants, so of course it starts with singing. Its first words are om ity etad aksharam udgitham upasita. Roughly: meditate on this syllable, om, as the udgitha. The high song and the sacred syllable are one. Then the text builds a ladder of essences. The essence of all these beings is the earth. Of earth, water. Of water, plants. Of plants, the human person. Of the person, speech. Of speech, the verses of the Rig Veda. Of the verses, the chant of the Sama Veda. And the essence of the chant is the udgitha, which is om. Then comes the line the whole day turns on: the udgitha is rasanam rasatamah, the essence of essences, the highest, the eighth rung. Rasa means juice, sap, flavor, the best part of a thing. Follow it down again: soil, rain, rice, a person, a voice, a verse, a song, a single syllable. In the text's picture, a person, boiled down, ends in a sound. That's the Upanishad's move, and you'll see it all year: it takes something the priests already did, a song at a fire, and asks what it means on the inside. The ritual stays. The meaning goes deeper. Om still opens prayer, study and puja in Hindu homes and temples today, and this chapter is one place that asks why.
screen: `THE VEDA OF CHANTS BEGINS WITH A SONG.` · `OM AND THE HIGH SONG ARE ONE.` · `A LADDER: EARTH TO WATER TO PERSON.` · `THE ESSENCE OF ESSENCES.` · then, large: `RASANAM RASATAMAH.`

segments.voice: Climb the ladder in your mind: the ground under you, the water you drank today, the food it grew, your body made from that food, your voice. If you'd like, let one soft om come out on the breath, or simply hear it inside, and notice it begin, swell and fade. Then rest in the quiet after it, the way the text rests at the top of its ladder.
The udgitha. The high song of the Sama Veda priests, which the Chandogya identifies with om and calls the essence of essences.
Your line: the essence. The best part of a thing, its rasa, is where this text always looks. Year two has begun.

screen: `DAY 332 COUNTS.` → `YEAR TWO, BEGUN.` → `TOMORROW: SPEECH AND BREATH ARGUE.`

333.title: Speech and breath argue about who is greatest (1.2)
333.hook: the senses quarrel over which of them matters most, and they settle it by leaving the body one at a time
333.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice pranayama, the regulation of breath, as part of daily worship and yoga; teachers sometimes tell this story of breath as the chief of the senses alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the udgitha, om, the essence of essences: earth, water, plants, person, speech, verse, chant, om. Your line was the essence.

Sooner or later, every team has this argument. The one who talks to the clients says the company runs on them. The one who builds the product says nothing exists without them. The planner says without a plan it's all chaos. Everyone is a little bit right, and nobody wants to hear it. The Chandogya Upanishad tells the same fight, only the team is inside your own body: speech, the eye, the ear, the mind and the breath, arguing over which of them is the greatest. The way they settle it is brilliant, and a little brutal.
screen: `EVERY TEAM HAS THIS ARGUMENT.` → `THE TEAM IS YOUR BODY.` → `WHO IS THE GREATEST?`

segments.voice: They go to Prajapati, the lord of creatures, and ask him to judge. His test: the greatest is the one whose leaving makes the body worst off. So they take turns walking out. Speech leaves for a whole year. Back again, it asks: how did you manage without me? Like someone who can't speak, the others say. We breathed, we saw, we heard, we thought. We got by. The eye leaves for a year, and they get by like someone who can't see. The ear leaves, and they live like someone who can't hear. The mind leaves, and they live, the text says, like small children whose minds haven't grown yet. Each time, the body carries on. Then breath gets ready to go. And here's the picture that makes the story stick: as a strong horse, pulling away, tears up the pegs it was tethered to, the breath begins to tear up all the others with it. Speech, eye, ear and mind come running. Stay, they say. You're the greatest of us. That full story sits in chapter five of the Chandogya. In chapter one, the passage the outline points to, a shorter story makes the same point: gods and demons fight, and the demons spoil speech, eye, ear and mind with evil. But when they strike the breath in the mouth, the chief breath, they shatter like a clod of earth thrown at a rock. In both places, breath holds the rest. And chapter five ends by saying people don't call the senses speech, eyes, ears and minds. They call them all pranas, breaths.
screen: `PRAJAPATI'S TEST: WHO CAN LEAVE?` · `SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: THE BODY GETS BY.` · `THE HORSE TEARS UP ITS PEGS.` · `THE SENSES ARE CALLED BREATHS.` · then, large: `STAY. YOU'RE THE GREATEST.`

segments.voice: Give the senses the day off: let your eyes close, let the room's sounds fall to the background, stay silent, and let thoughts drift past without chasing them. Then notice what's still going without being asked, in and out, the one the others ran back to. Just keep it company.
Prana, life-breath. When breath prepares to leave the body, like a strong horse tearing up its tethering pegs, speech, eye, ear and mind come running, calling it the greatest of them all.
Your line: breath wins. The others can step out for a year; breath holds them all. Day three hundred thirty-three, done.

334.title: The dog's udgitha — satire of empty ritual (1.12)
334.hook: a pack of dogs files in like priests, sits down, and chants: om, let us eat; om, let us drink
334.tomorrow: Satyakama, the boy who told the truth
334.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often stress bhava, the inner feeling behind worship, alongside correct form; many families teach children both the words of a prayer and what it means.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prana, and your line, breath wins. The senses walked out one by one, but when breath pulled away like a horse tearing up its pegs, they all came running back.

A student walks out of the village to study the Veda somewhere quiet, and a white dog appears in front of him. Other dogs gather around the white dog and say to it: sir, sing for us, and get us some food. We're hungry. The white dog says: come back here tomorrow morning. The student, understandably, stays to watch. Next morning the dogs return, and what they do is not what you'd expect to find in a book of sacred chant.
screen: `A STUDENT GOES TO STUDY.` → `A WHITE DOG, AND A HUNGRY PACK.` → `COME BACK TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: The dogs come in a line, each holding on to the one ahead, the way the priests moved together when they entered to sing a particular chant. They sit down. They make the chant's opening sound, hin. Then they sing, in the same form the priests used for the high song we met two days ago. Om, let us eat. Om, let us drink. Om, may the gods bring food here. Lord of food, bring food here, bring it. Om. That's the whole hymn. Two days ago the Chandogya called the udgitha the essence of essences, the top of a ladder that runs from earth to om. Now a pack of dogs uses the exact same chant to ask for breakfast. Many modern scholars read the passage as satire: a sharp joke at priests who sang the sacred song mainly for the fee and the meal that came with it. The words were right. The form was right. What was missing was the inside, the meditation the first chapter asked for. Not everyone reads it as a joke. Some traditional commentators take the dogs as sages or gods in disguise, come to teach the student. The text doesn't explain itself, so both readings stay open. Either way, the question lands on anyone who has said grace while thinking about dessert, or sung a hymn while checking the time. You can do every outward step of a ritual and still be chanting for food alone.

segments.voice: Take one small thing you do by habit, a prayer before meals, lighting a lamp, even washing your hands, and go through it slowly in your mind, step by step. At each step ask, not what do I get, but what is this for? If you pray, say one familiar line slowly, hearing each word, and then simply rest.

335.title: Satyakama, the boy who told the truth about his mother (4.4)
335.hook: a boy asks his mother who his father was; she doesn't know, and he carries that answer, word for word, to his teacher
335.tomorrow: the bull, the fire, the swan, the bird
335.howItsDone: Satyakama's story is told to Hindu children as a lesson in honesty, and teachers cite it when discussing whether spiritual standing comes from birth or from character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: udgitha, and a pack of dogs chanting om, let us eat. Your line was don't chant for food alone: right form, missing inside.

Name. Date of birth. Father's name. On plenty of old forms, that third line sat near the top, and for some people it was the hardest line on the page. In the Chandogya, a boy who wants to study the Veda faces the spoken version of that line. A teacher will ask: what is your family, your lineage? So the boy, Satyakama, goes home first and asks his mother.
screen: `FATHER'S NAME: ______.` → `WHAT IS YOUR LINEAGE?` → `A BOY ASKS HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: His mother's name is Jabala, and she answers him honestly. I don't know your lineage, my son. When I was young, I moved about a great deal working as a servant, and that's when I had you. But I am Jabala, and you are Satyakama. So call yourself Satyakama Jabala: a name made from his mother, not his father. The boy walks to the teacher, Haridrumata Gautama, and asks to become his student. The teacher asks: what is your lineage, my dear? And Satyakama repeats his mother's words, all of them, the part that might shame her and the part that might shut him out. I don't know, sir. My mother says she moved about as a servant when she was young, and had me then. She is Jabala, I am Satyakama. I'm Satyakama Jabala. The teacher's reply is the hinge of the story. No one but a true brahmin could speak like that, he says. Fetch the firewood, my dear. I'll take you as a student. You have not gone away from the truth. Look at what counts as the qualification here. Not birth. Not a famous father. The truth, told when a lie would have been easier. His very name holds it: satya means truth, kama means desire. Satyakama, the one who loves truth. Hindus have read this story in different ways. For some, it shows that character is what a brahmin really is. Others, including some traditional commentators, read the teacher as concluding that a boy this truthful must be of brahmin birth after all. Either way, the story keeps the boy at the door, saying I don't know, out loud.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW, MY SON.` · `SATYAKAMA, SON OF JABALA.` · `HE REPEATS IT ALL TO THE TEACHER.` · `YOU HAVE NOT GONE FROM THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `SATYA, TRUTH. KAMA, DESIRE.`

segments.voice: Settle into the breath and think of one true thing about yourself that you usually leave out: something you don't know, something you aren't, a part of your story you skip. You don't have to tell anyone; just let it be true here, without dressing it up or explaining it away. Notice whether it feels heavier hidden, or lighter said.
Satyakama. The one who loves truth: a boy without a known father, accepted as a student because he told the truth at the door.
Your line: truth is the qualification. A boy with no lineage to give had exactly that. See you tomorrow.

336.title: The bull, the fire, the swan, the bird teach Satyakama (4.5–4.8)
336.hook: sent off with four hundred thin cows, Satyakama is taught by the herd's bull, the evening fire, a swan and a diving bird
336.howItsDone: Cows, rivers, fire and the directions all have places in Hindu worship, and teachers tell Satyakama's story to show that learning can come from anywhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Satyakama, the boy who said I don't know at the teacher's door. Your line was truth is the qualification. Today ends the first week of year two.

Satyakama has been accepted. You'd expect his first lesson to be a verse, a chant, a teaching by the fire. Instead his teacher picks out four hundred cows, thin and weak, and says: look after these. Satyakama doesn't complain. I won't come back, he says, until they're a thousand. He drives them off into the forest and stays away for years. No teacher. No books. Just cows, grass and sky. And out there, alone, the lessons start arriving, from teachers nobody would have chosen.
screen: `FOUR HUNDRED THIN COWS.` → `NOT BACK UNTIL A THOUSAND.` → `ALONE IN THE FOREST FOR YEARS.`

segments.voice: When the herd reaches a thousand, the bull speaks. Satyakama, we're a thousand now. Take us home, and let me tell you one quarter of Brahman, the great reality. The bull names the four directions, east, west, south, north, and calls that quarter the shining. The fire, it says, will tell him the next. That evening Satyakama lights the fire and pens the cows, and the fire speaks: earth, the air between, the sky, the ocean. That quarter is the endless. The next evening a swan flies down: fire, sun, moon, lightning. The luminous. The evening after, a diving water bird: breath, eye, ear, mind. The quarter that has a home. Four teachers, four quarters: the directions, the worlds, the lights, and his own body. He reaches his teacher's house, and the teacher looks at him and says: your face shines like someone who knows Brahman. Who taught you? Beings other than people, Satyakama answers. But please, teach me yourself. His teacher does, and the text says nothing was left out. Now the week, from the top. Day one, om, the essence of essences. Day two, the senses argue, and breath wins. Day three, dogs chanting for breakfast. Day four, a boy telling the truth at the door. Today, a bull, a fire, a swan and a bird. One thread runs through them: the Chandogya finds the sacred beyond the altar as well as on it, in the breath, the truth, the herd and the evening fire.
screen: `THE BULL: THE FOUR DIRECTIONS.` · `THE FIRE, THE SWAN, THE DIVING BIRD.` · `YOUR FACE SHINES. WHO TAUGHT YOU?` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Notice the direction you're facing and the ones behind and beside you, the bull's quarter; then the ground and the air above it, the fire's; then whatever light is around you, the swan's. Come home to your breath, your eyes, your ears and your mind, the diving bird's. No need to hear any voices; just let each one be a teacher for a few breaths.
The bull. The first of Satyakama's four unlikely teachers, who names the four directions as the shining quarter of Brahman.
Your line: the whole world teaches. Even a bull, a swan and an evening fire. Week one of year two, done.
